newsitem.title: INDIA: India reacts calmly to Bhutto dismissal.
newsitem.headline: India reacts calmly to Bhutto dismissal.

text.p: India reacted calmly on Tuesday to the sacking of Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto in neighbouring Pakistan, with whom it has fought three wars in the nearly 50 years the two countries have been independent.

Senior members of an Indian delegation in Zimbabwe with Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda told India's Asian News International (ANI) agency that Bhutto's dismissal was an internal affair and India had no comment.
The delegation was in Harare for an economic meeting.
"If our assessment is correct, the Pakistani government would not have been dismissed without the army's blessing," a defence official in New Delhi said.
"Our perception is that the current army leadership in Pakistan does not favour military adventurism against India.

Pakistani President Farooq Leghari dismissed Bhutto's government on Tuesday, accusing it of corruption and misrule in what appears to have been a planned action that had army support and was within his constitutional powers.
The military kept a low profile. But political observers said the president could not have acted without the approval and cooperation of the generals.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since independence from Britain in 1947 and they have not held official talks for more than two years.
Indian diplomats said they did not expect an interim governnment in Pakistan to resume the talks, mainly over the Himalayan region of Kashmir -- the cause of two of the wars.
"It is not Pakistani governments but the Pakistani establishment that determines ties with India," one diplomat told Reuters. "That establishment remains very much intact."
An Indian interior ministry official said the change in Pakistan was unlikely to make any difference to India.

"Basically, the situation will not affect us in any important way. If the government has been dismissed to check instability, and if fresh elections are held soon, we have no worries," the official said.

Former Indian foreign secretary Jyotindra Nath Dixit, the last Indian official to hold formal talks with Pakistan, said Bhutto's dismissal followed a growing list of complaints against her, including a troubled economy.
Dixit said he had known Pakistan's army chief, General Jehangir Karamat, during his time as Indian high commissioner (ambassador) in Islamabad.
"It seems that Farooq Leghari and Karamat will rule the roost," he said.
He said Karamat did not appear to be an anti-India militarist.
"He was not the sort of person who would try to seek a military solution to the problems with India.
"The decision to dismiss Bhutto was probably taken after the intelligence agencies decided that the opposition campaign against her could not be contained without her removal," Dixit added.
